items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most transformative technological innovations of the twenty-first century, fundamentally changing the way individuals learn, work, communicate, and solve complex problems. Although AI has become a prominent component of modern society only in recent decades, its conceptual foundations extend back several centuries through philosophical discussions concerning human intelligence, logical reasoning, and mechanical computation. The evolution of Artificial Intelligence represents a multidisciplinary journey involving computer science, mathematics, cognitive psychology, neuroscience, linguistics, philosophy, engineering, statistics, and data science. Continuous advancements in computational power, algorithmic development, data availability, and digital infrastructure have enabled AI to evolve from theoretical concepts into intelligent systems capable of performing tasks that traditionally required human intelligence. The earliest ideas related to artificial intelligence originated long before the invention of computers. Ancient civilizations imagined intelligent machines capable of mimicking human behaviour through myths, literature, and mechanical inventions. During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, philosophers and mathematicians such as René Descartes, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, and George Boole contributed foundational concepts related to logic, reasoning, symbolic representation, and mathematical computation. Their work laid the intellectual groundwork for the development of computational systems capable of representing knowledge and making logical decisions.The modern evolution of Artificial Intelligence began during the twentieth century with the rapid advancement of computing technologies. In the 1930s and 1940s, significant progress in mathematical logic and computer science established the theoretical basis for intelligent machines. Alan Turing introduced the concept of a universal computing machine and later proposed the famous Turing Test, which examined whether a machine could demonstrate behaviour indistinguishable from that of a human being. Turing's pioneering contributions remain fundamental to contemporary AI research because they established that machines could potentially perform intelligent reasoning through computational processes. A major milestone occurred in 1956 during the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, organized by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon, and Nathaniel Rochester. This conference formally introduced the term "Artificial Intelligence" and established AI as an independent scientific discipline. Researchers believed that human intelligence could be represented computationally and that machines could eventually perform reasoning, learning, language understanding, and problem-solving. The Dartmouth Conference inspired widespread academic interest and initiated decades of intensive research into intelligent computing systems.The period between the late 1950s and early 1970s is often referred to as the early development phase of Artificial Intelligence. During this era, researchers developed symbolic AI methods that emphasized logical reasoning, rule-based systems, theorem proving, and problem-solving algorithms. Early AI programmes successfully solved mathematical problems, played strategic games such as chess, and demonstrated limited natural language capabilities. Optimism surrounding AI research increased substantially as scientists believed that general human-level intelligence could be achieved within a relatively short period. However, limitations in computing power, data availability, memory capacity, and algorithmic efficiency restricted further progress. During the 1970s and 1980s, Artificial Intelligence experienced periods commonly known as the "AI Winters," characterized by reduced research funding, slower technological progress, and diminished public expectations. Many ambitious predictions regarding human-level machine intelligence proved unrealistic because available computing resources and algorithms were insufficient to support increasingly complex AI applications. Despite these challenges, important research continued in knowledge representation, expert systems, machine learning, robotics, and computational reasoning. Expert systems became particularly successful by capturing specialized human knowledge through rule-based decision-making frameworks that supported medical diagnosis, engineering design, financial analysis, and industrial management.The late 1980s and 1990s marked the gradual resurgence of Artificial Intelligence through the development of machine learning approaches. Rather than relying exclusively on manually programmed rules, researchers began designing algorithms capable of learning patterns directly from data. Statistical modelling, neural networks, evolutionary computation, fuzzy logic, probabilistic reasoning, and support vector machines expanded the capabilities of intelligent systems while improving adaptability, prediction accuracy, and decision-making performance. Significant improvements in computational hardware further accelerated AI research during this period. A landmark achievement occurred in 1997 when IBM's Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov, demonstrating the ability of intelligent computing systems to outperform human experts in highly specialized domains. This achievement attracted worldwide attention and illustrated the practical potential of Artificial Intelligence beyond theoretical research. Similar advances subsequently appeared in speech recognition, computer vision, autonomous robotics, medical diagnosis, financial forecasting, and industrial automation.The twenty-first century has witnessed unprecedented growth in Artificial Intelligence driven by three major technological developments: the availability of massive digital datasets, substantial improvements in computational processing power, and the emergence of advanced machine learning algorithms. The rapid expansion of the internet, cloud computing, mobile technologies, social media, and digital services generated enormous volumes of data that enabled intelligent systems to learn more effectively. Simultaneously, Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), high-performance computing, and cloud-based infrastructure significantly accelerated AI model training and deployment across diverse application domains. Deep learning has become one of the most influential developments in contemporary Artificial Intelligence. Inspired by the structure of the human brain, deep neural networks consist of multiple computational layers capable of learning complex representations from large datasets. These architectures have dramatically improved performance in image recognition, speech processing, language translation, autonomous driving, medical imaging, recommendation systems, fraud detection, and scientific research. Deep learning has transformed Artificial Intelligence from narrow task-specific applications into highly sophisticated systems capable of addressing increasingly complex real-world challenges.Natural Language Processing (NLP) has experienced remarkable advancement through transformer architectures and large language models capable of understanding, generating, summarizing, translating, and analysing human language with unprecedented accuracy. Conversational AI systems, intelligent virtual assistants, multilingual communication platforms, automated content generation, and research support tools have become integral components of education, healthcare, business, governance, and scientific research. These developments have substantially enhanced human-computer interaction while expanding opportunities for intelligent educational technologies. The emergence of generative Artificial Intelligence represents another significant milestone in AI evolution. Modern generative models can produce text, images, computer code, audio, video, simulations, educational content, and scientific documentation while supporting creativity, innovation, research, and personalized learning. These technologies have transformed knowledge creation and digital communication by enabling collaborative interactions between humans and intelligent systems across numerous professional disciplines.Artificial Intelligence has evolved beyond isolated computational applications into a foundational technology supporting digital transformation across multiple sectors. Healthcare employs AI for disease diagnosis, medical imaging, drug discovery, personalized treatment, and patient monitoring. Manufacturing integrates AI with robotics, predictive maintenance, quality control, and smart production systems. Financial institutions utilize intelligent algorithms for fraud detection, risk management, investment analysis, and customer services. Agriculture benefits from precision farming, crop monitoring, environmental analysis, and resource optimization. Transportation increasingly relies upon autonomous vehicles, intelligent traffic management, and logistics optimization. Education has emerged as one of the fastest-growing application areas where Artificial Intelligence supports personalized learning, intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment, curriculum development, learning analytics, educational administration, and lifelong learning. items.title: From assistance to dependence: The nexus between AI dependence and workplace cognitive engagement
items.abstract: Background The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) tools into workplace practices has reshaped how employees process information and perform cognitive tasks. While these systems are often associated with superior efficiency, their excessive use may entail significant cognitive costs. Objective Grounded in automation complacency perspective and the growing literature on technology addiction, this study investigates how dependence on artificial intelligence is associated with cognitive engagement in the workplace, with particular attention to the mediating role of cognitive fatigue. Methods Adopting quantitative research design, data were collected from 246 academic and administrative staff who actively use AI tools in their daily work routines. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) was used to test the theoretical model proposed. Results The findings indicate that dependence on AI was positively associated with cognitive fatigue (β = 0.569; t = 13.468; p = 0.000) and negatively with cognitive engagement (β = −0.174; t = 2.503; p = 0.012). In addition, the relationship between cognitive fatigue and cognitive engagement was found to be negative and statistically significant (β = −0.207; t = 2.773; p = 0.006). Mediation analysis further revealed that cognitive fatigue partially mediates the relationship between dependence on AI and cognitive engagement (indirect effect β = −0.118, t = 2.724, p < .01; VAF = 40.5%). Conclusion These results suggest that higher levels of dependence on AI correspond to higher employee cognitive fatigue, which in turn relates to lower cognitive engagement at work. By empirically demonstrating the cognitive costs of AI reliance, this study contributes to the emerging literature on workplace AI and technology addiction.

items.title: From automation to generative artificial intelligence: Human-AI co-creativity in professional communication: A structured literature synthesis
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines the transition from automation to generative AI in professional communication, focusing on human–AI co-creativity. While earlier research framed AI mainly as an efficiency tool, the rapid emergence of generative AI has reconfigured communication practices toward collaborative and co-creative models. This structured literature synthesis, informed by PRISMA reporting principles, synthesizes empirical research published between 2012 and 2026 across journalism, public relations, strategic communication, and digital media, investigating how generative AI is integrated into creative workflows and how communicative agency is distributed between human professionals and AI systems. The results identify four dimensions shaping human–AI co-creativity: (1) AI affordances enabling ideation while introducing constraints such as algorithmic opacity; (2) human professional agency, through which practitioners retain interpretive authority via prompt design; (3) organizational context, structuring AI adoption; and (4) ethical and cultural norms concerning transparency and accountability. The review advances conceptual clarity on human–AI co-creativity as an emergent sociotechnical process, arguing that generative AI is not simply augmenting communication work but fundamentally reshaping how creativity, authorship, and responsibility are enacted. Key Words: Generative Artificial Intelligence, Co-Creativity, Professional Communication, PRISMA, Human–AI Collaboration About the Authors * Tommy Kibera Kiilu, Ph.D., is a Lecturer in the Department of Communication, Media, Film and Theatre Studies at Kenyatta University, Nairobi, Kenya where he was Chairperson of the Department from 2020–2025. He also has industry experience in marketing and brand strategy from Rome. His scholarly work focuses on media studies, development and strategic communication, with particular interest in artificial intelligence in journalism, media ethics, digital transformation, and media literacy. ** Martin Kuria Githinji, Ph.D. is a Lecturer in the Department of Communication, Media, Film, and Theatre Studies at Kenyatta University, Nairobi, Kenya, holding a PhD in Communication Studies and specializing in digital media, strategic, and crisis communication, with particular attention to the Global South. items.title: From Automation to Human Touch: A Bibliometric Analysis of Chatbot Anthropomorphism and Purchase Intention
items.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence–driven chatbots into digital commerce has transformed firm–consumer interactions, shifting the focus from efficiency-oriented automation toward more human-centered engagement. In this context, anthropomorphic chatbot design has emerged as a key mechanism through which firms seek to introduce human touch into AI-mediated interactions and influence consumer purchase intention. Despite growing scholarly attention, existing research on chatbot anthropomorphism remains fragmented across disciplines, limiting a comprehensive understanding of its intellectual structure, theoretical foundations, and thematic evolution. To address this gap, the present study conducts a PRISMA 2020–guided bibliometric and systematic review of research published between 2016 and 2025. Drawing on a bibliometric dataset of 200 publications and a systematically screened subset of 80 high-quality studies, the analysis employs VOSviewer to examine publication trends, keyword co-occurrence patterns, and co-authorship networks. The findings reveal a clear progression in the literature from automation-focused chatbot applications toward human-centered AI interactions emphasizing anthropomorphism, social presence, and relational mechanisms. The results identify anthropomorphic design, human touch, trust, and consumer engagement as central themes shaping purchase intention in chatbot-mediated environments. By integrating anthropomorphism theory, social presence theory, and the Computers as Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, the study proposes a theory-driven framework explaining how human-like chatbot cues activate perceptions of human touch, which subsequently foster trust and influence consumer buying behavior. Beyond consolidating fragmented literature, this study advances theoretical understanding of human-centered AI and offers actionable insights for managers seeking to design effective chatbot interactions in digital commerce. The findings also highlight promising avenues for future research, including contextual, cross cultural, and ethical considerations in anthropomorphic AI design.

items.title: From Bayt Al-Hikmah to The Era of Artificial Intelligence (AI): Epistemological Transformation of Knowledge and Its Relevance for Scientific Integration in Islamic Education
items.abstract: The transformation of knowledge from the classical Islamic tradition to the modern era and Artificial Intelligence (AI) demonstrates not only the growth of knowledge but also shifts in its sources, methods, validity, and authority. However, studies on Bayt al-Hikmah, the development of modern science, Islamic epistemology, and AI in Islamic education tend to be discussed in separate domains. Consequently, the connection between these epistemological transformations and scientific integration in Islamic education has not been systematically examined. This study aims to analyze the epistemological transformation of knowledge from classical scholarly traditions through Bayt al-Hikmah, the development of modern science, to the AI era, and to examine its relevance to scientific integration in Islamic education. This study employs a qualitative approach with a library research method. Literature was analyzed descriptively and analytically across four dimensions: sources, methods, validity, and authority of knowledge. The findings indicate that Bayt al-Hikmah represents an open scientific paradigm toward various traditions through translation, dialogue, critique, and knowledge development. Modern science subsequently reinforced scientific methods, observation, experimentation, and empirical proof, though the rise of specialization also risks driving scientific fragmentation. The contribution of this study lies in its continuous reading of these transformations through four epistemological dimensions and their connection to the integrative-interconnective paradigm in Islamic education. In this context, scientific integration needs to connect revelation, reason, empirical experience, technology, and ethical and spiritual values. AI should be positioned as an instrument for knowledge development that remains subject to human verification, interpretation, and ethical judgment.

items.title: From Context to Plasticity: A Three-Timescale Architecture for Persistent Memory and Recursive Online Learning
items.abstract: This work presents a theoretical architecture for continually adapting AI systems organized around three distinct timescales: (1) fast transformer key-value context for immediate interaction, (2) medium-term persistent recurrent memory with decaying importance and consolidation, and (3) slow, controlled parameter adaptation. The proposed pathway is context → persistent memory → importance estimation → consolidation → plasticity gating → bounded parameter update → changed future computation. The manuscript formalizes recurrent state dynamics, transformer attention, gated persistent memory, exponential importance decay, importance-biased retrieval, prediction loss, gated online updates, consolidation thresholds, and learned update rules. It also explains why adapting recurrent transition weights such as U changes state-transition dynamics, whereas updating memory changes stored state without necessarily changing the underlying transition rule. The package distinguishes inference-time state adaptation, memory adaptation, online parameter learning, meta-learning, recursive self-learning, and recursive self-improvement. It proposes controlled experiments comparing transformer, KV-context, persistent-memory, importance, consolidation, gated-update, and learned-update variants, with metrics for retention, transfer, forgetting, poisoning robustness, parameter drift, retrieval quality, and compute cost. This is a conceptual research architecture and falsifiable research hypothesis. It reports no experimental measurements and does not claim AGI, consciousness, human-level cognition, biological equivalence, or open-ended recursive self-improvement. The prefrontal-cortex comparison is functional only, referring to working-memory maintenance, goal persistence, error monitoring, and adaptive control. AI assistance disclosure: ChatGPT assisted with manuscript drafting, mathematical editing, structure, and package preparation. Final authorship and publication decisions remain with Chaman Prakash Kanth. Sarvam AI was also used.

items.title: From Dependence To Independence: Work, Economy, And The Changing Future Of Work In English Literature With Special Reference To Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre, Elizabeth Gaskell's North And South And Virginia Woolf's A Room Of One's Own
items.abstract: Literature is a mirror of society. It shows the economic conditions, social problems, and daily struggles of human life across different times. Work is one of the most important parts of human life. In the past, many people depended completely on land, rich masters, or family heads for their survival. Over time, the meaning of work has changed from total dependence to economic independence. English literature presents many stories of characters who fight against poverty and social rules to earn their own living and live with dignity. Work is not just a way to earn money; it also gives a person self-respect, identity, and personal freedom. This research paper examines how work, economy, and independence are presented in selected English literary texts: Charlotte Brontë’s Jane Eyre, Elizabeth Gaskell’s North and South, and Virginia Woolf’s A Room of One’s Own. These texts show how education, employment, and money help individuals to become free and confident. Finally, this paper connects these literary lessons with the modern world. Today, technology, artificial intelligence, online platforms, and work-from-home jobs are changing the future of work. The paper concludes that even in the modern digital age, human dignity and economic security are essential for true freedom.

items.title: From Digital Libraries to Intelligent Knowledge Hubs: Reimagining Libraries for Viksit Bharat @2047
items.abstract: The evolution of digital technologies has fundamentally transformed the role of libraries in society. Libraries that were once physical repositories of printed material are now providing greater access to e-books, e-journals, digital repositories, online databases, and institutional resources. The next frontier in this evolution is the creation of intelligent knowledge hubs, enabled by new technologies such as Artificial Intelligence, machine learning, cloud computing, natural language processing, and multilingual systems. Intelligent libraries have the potential to be critical knowledge infrastructures for education, research, innovation, digital literacy, skill development, and lifelong learning in the context of Viksit Bharat @2047. Digital resources and remote information services can help bridge the knowledge divide between rural and urban communities, while multilingual digital content can enhance information access for a diverse range of users. At the same time, the development of intelligent knowledge hubs also presents a number of challenges, including inadequate digital infrastructure, financial constraints, skills gaps, data privacy, cybersecurity, copyright, and ethical issues around AI. Consequently, technological development needs to be supported by well-trained library professionals, robust security measures, ethical practices, and user-focused policies. By taking an inclusive and sustainable approach, intelligent libraries can play a significant role in advancing a knowledge-driven, digitally empowered, and inclusive Viksit Bharat @2047

items.title: From Gatekeepers to Gatekeeping Systems: Rethinking Journalism Theory in the Age of Algorithms and Generative AI
items.abstract: Abstract : Gatekeeping has remained one of the foundational theoretical approaches for explaining how information becomes news. From Kurt Lewin’s conceptualisation of gates and channels to David Manning White’s study of the newspaper wire editor, traditional gatekeeping theory located considerable power in human actors who selected, rejected and organised information before it reached audiences. The contemporary news environment, however, complicates this model. News selection is increasingly distributed across journalists, newsroom analytics, search engines, social media platforms, recommender systems and generative artificial intelligence. This paper re-examines gatekeeping theory through an interdisciplinary synthesis of journalism studies, platform studies, artificial intelligence research and communication theory. Drawing on a structured conceptual review of more than 29 major scholarly contributions, it argues that contemporary journalism is moving from identifiable gatekeepers towards interconnected gatekeeping systems. Within these systems, editorial judgement has not disappeared; rather, it interacts continuously with computational selection, platform infrastructures, audience behaviour and generative systems capable of producing, summarising and reorganising information. The paper proposes a five-layer model of contemporary gatekeeping comprising source, editorial, algorithmic, platform and generative gates. It further distinguishes between selection power, traditionally exercised by editors, and visibility power, increasingly exercised through technological infrastructures. The study concludes that gatekeeping theory remains valuable but requires conceptual expansion from the question of who controls the gate to the broader question of how interconnected human and computational systems determine what information becomes visible, credible and socially consequential.

items.title: From GenAI-enabled knowledge creation to SME digital transformation: the mediating role of entrepreneurial innovativeness
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-enabled knowledge creation processes influence entrepreneurial knowledge co-creation and small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) digital transformation through entrepreneurial general innovativeness and entrepreneurial specific innovativeness. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the socialization, externalization, combination and internalization (SECI) knowledge creation framework, the study develops and tests a mediation model linking GenAI internalization (GAI), GenAI externalization (GAE), GenAI socialization (GAS) and GenAI combination (GAC) with SME outcomes. Data was collected from 391 SME respondents and analysed using covariance-based structural equation modelling in analysis of moment structures. Findings The findings show that GAI, GAE and GAC significantly enhance both entrepreneurial general innovativeness and entrepreneurial specific innovativeness. GAS significantly influences entrepreneurial specific innovativeness but does not significantly affect entrepreneurial general innovativeness. Both forms of entrepreneurial innovativeness positively influence entrepreneurial knowledge co-creation and SME digital transformation. Mediation results further show that entrepreneurial general innovativeness mediates the effects of GAI, GAE and GAC, while entrepreneurial specific innovativeness provides a more consistent mediating pathway across GenAI-enabled knowledge processes. Practical implications SME managers should use GenAI not merely for automation or content generation, but for learning, knowledge articulation, knowledge integration, innovation adoption and digital transformation. Originality/value The study advances GenAI entrepreneurship research by showing how GenAI-enabled SECI processes create SME value through entrepreneurial innovativeness.

items.title: From Life Preservation to Global Normative Orientation: The New Human Rights and the Semantic Field of Jean-Pol Martin
items.abstract: This working paper develops the worldwide normative claim of Jean-Pol Martin’s New Human Rights (NMR) and semantic field. It examines how an organismic understanding of human life, basic needs and collective problem-solving can inform standards for education, institutions, community development and human-AI cooperation. The argument makes the normative bridge explicit: when the preservation and flourishing of human life, equal consideration of persons and the protection of shared life-supporting conditions are accepted as aims, societal decisions should be assessed by their effects on those conditions. The six NMR domains are thinking, health, security, social inclusion, self-realization and participation, and meaning. The New Human Rights articulate rights and aims; the semantic field provides a connected vocabulary for understanding situations, evaluating alternatives and organizing cooperative action. What this article adds:Normative orientation is already present in the existing framework. This paper’s specific contribution is its focused justification of worldwide normative use. It distinguishes anthropological description, normative commitments and institutional implications, and illustrates their connection through the participatory redesign of a public square. Function within the Zenodo corpus:The article connects the reconstruction of Martin’s theory architecture with public justification and practical decision criteria. It links existing strands on Learning by Teaching, New Human Rights, semantic coherence, prioritization, governance and human-AI cooperation. It thus serves as a bridge from conceptual synthesis to accountable societal application. Worldwide orientation is understood as shared evaluative concerns combined with context-sensitive implementation. The paper proposes a framework for public discussion and application; it does not claim existing international endorsement or legal recognition of the NMR. This is a conceptual working paper without a new empirical dataset. Jean-Pol Martin supplied the conceptual framework and direction. ChatGPT assisted with argument development, English drafting and layout.

items.title: From Ratings to Sensors: Real-Time AIIoT-Based Credibility Anchored on Blockchain for Ride-Sharing Ecosystems
items.abstract: Current ride-sharing platforms predominantly rely on subjective post-ride ratings to evaluate driver credibility, making reputation systems vulnerable to user bias, delayed feedback, collusion, and manipulation. Although recent studies have explored blockchain-based ride-sharing, AI-driven driver monitoring, and IoT-enabled transportation independently, they do not provide an integrated trust framework that continuously derives credibility from objectively verifiable driving behaviour while maintaining scalability and low operational cost.This paper presents Ridezy, a decentralized trust architecture that replaces conventional rating-based reputation with real-time sensor-driven credibility. The proposed framework combines edge Artificial Intelligence and Internet of Things (AIIoT) technologies to continuously monitor behavioural indicators such as lane discipline, speed compliance, braking behaviour, and traffic sign adherence. Instead of storing high-frequency telemetry on the blockchain, Ridezy employs a hybrid architecture in which behavioural summaries are processed off-chain and only cryptographic hashes, credibility updates, and payment records are anchored on Polygon smart contracts, enabling tamper-evident trust with minimal blockchain overhead. To evaluate the proposed architecture, Ridezy is compared against three representative trust models: a traditional rating-based system, an AI-only architecture, and a blockchain-only architecture. The evaluation considers behavioural detection performance, end-to-end latency, cost efficiency, throughput, reputation stability, tamper resistance, and component-wise ablation studies. Experimental results demonstrate that the hybrid architecture achieves higher behavioural fidelity and stronger trust guarantees than conventional reputation mechanisms while maintaining low per-ride blockchain cost and scalable operation through batched on-chain commitments.The primary contribution of this work is a sensor-driven credibility framework that transforms real-time behavioural evidence into a cryptographically verifiable trust primitive for ride-sharing ecosystems. By combining edge AI, IoT telemetry, and blockchain-based trust anchoring within a scalable hybrid architecture, Ridezy provides a practical foundation for trustworthy, transparent, and next-generation intelligent mobility systems.

items.title: Future Trends
items.abstract: AI is rapidly transforming the educational landscape, and its future impact is expected to extend beyond individual learning tools toward broader changes in teaching, assessment, institutional management, research, and educational ecosystems. Future developments may create increasingly intelligent and personalized learning environments in which humans and AI systems work together to support educational goals. The year 2035 represents an important horizon for considering the future development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education. By this period, AI may become deeply integrated into learning platforms, educational administration, research environments, assessment systems, digital classrooms, and professional education. The future of education is unlikely to be based on AI alone. Instead, educational environments may increasingly combine AI capabilities with human expertise, creativity, emotional intelligence, critical thinking, and ethical responsibility. A possible framework is: AI Technology + Human Expertise + Digital Infrastructure + Ethical Governance = Future Education By 2035, AI may become a regular component of educational environments rather than an additional technological tool. Students may interact with intelligent learning systems that continuously adapt to their learning progress, interests, abilities, and educational goals. Teachers may use AI to support lesson planning, assessment, learning analytics, content development, and personalized instruction.

items.title: Fuzzy model for assessing digital security literacy across population groups with different social profiles
items.abstract: The article proposes a fuzzy model for assessing the level of digital security literacy of the population, considering socio-demographic characteristics. The relevance of the study is determined by the growth of cyber threats, digital risks, and the role of the human factor in ensuring the stability of the digital environment, which requires a transition from fragmentary measurements to comprehensive and interpretable assessment approaches. The scientific novelty of the work lies in combining the convolution method and fuzzy modelling to form integral quantitative and linguistic assessments of digital security literacy across various social profiles of the population. The proposed method makes it possible to formalize heterogeneous demographic and behavioural data, conduct profile-based analysis, and generate targeted analytical conclusions to support management decision-making. The practical significance of the study was confirmed by verifying the proposed method on real empirical data obtained from a questionnaire survey of 315 respondents in the Transcarpathian region. The verification showed that the proposed method provides a normalized quantitative assessment for a selected social profile with an integral value of 0.644, which corresponds to an above-average level of digital security literacy. Compared with simple averaging of the entire sample, the proposed method increases the analytical specificity of the assessment by enabling profile-oriented evaluation and targeted interpretation of results rather than only obtaining a generalized population-level indicator. The results obtained demonstrate the possibility of using the proposed method to assess the level of digital security literacy, segment the population by social profiles, identify vulnerable groups, and justify targeted educational and preventive measures. Prospects for further research are related to expanding the empirical base, automating data collection and processing procedures, integrating new assessment criteria, and analysing the dynamics of digital security literacy over time and across regions.

items.title: GAN-Enhanced Multimodal Artificial Intelligence for Autism Spectrum Disorder Screening: A Comprehensive Survey
items.abstract: Abstract Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by difficulties in social communication and interaction, together with restricted or repetitive patterns of behavior. Early screening is important for facilitating timely clinical assessment and intervention; however, conventional screening approaches often depend on clinical expertise, behavioral observation, developmental history, and standardized assessment tools. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have created new opportunities for data-driven and automated ASD screening. This survey provides a comprehensive review of AI-based approaches for ASD screening, with particular emphasis on multimodal learning and the integration of heterogeneous data sources. Behavioral, genetic, environmental, neuroimaging, physiological, and clinical data modalities are examined, along with approaches for combining information across multiple sources. The survey further reviews the role of GANs and related generative approaches in synthetic-data generation and data augmentation, particularly in addressing challenges associated with limited and imbalanced datasets. Multimodal fusion strategies, multi-input neural networks, and emerging deep learning approaches are also discussed in the context of ASD screening. The reviewed literature indicates that multimodal AI has the potential to provide a more comprehensive representation of ASD-related characteristics than single-modality approaches. However, important challenges remain, including limited and heterogeneous datasets, class imbalance, multimodal data integration, GAN training instability, synthetic-data quality, privacy and security, model interpretability, generalizability, and limited external clinical validation. This survey identifies these challenges and highlights research directions toward reliable, explainable, privacy-preserving, and clinically validated AI-based multimodal ASD screening systems. Keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD); Artificial Intelligence; Machine Learning; Deep Learning; Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs); Multimodal Learning; ASD Screening; Data Augmentation; Synthetic Data

items.title: GenAI-Net: A generative AI framework for automated biomolecular network design
items.abstract: Biomolecular networks underlie both natural biological processes and engineered cellular technologies, from intracellular regulation and ecological dynamics to biomanufacturing, smart therapeutics, and cell-based diagnostics. However, designing chemical reaction networks (CRNs) that implement a desired dynamical function remains a challenging task. Although candidate networks can be evaluated by simulation, the inverse problem of discovering networks from behavioral specifications remains difficult. It requires navigating vast spaces of topologies and kinetic parameters governed by nonlinear and potentially stochastic dynamics. Here, we introduce GenAI-Net, a generative artificial intelligence framework that automates CRN design by coupling reaction proposal to simulation-based evaluation defined by a user-specified objective. GenAI-Net efficiently produces topologically diverse solutions across design tasks, including dose-response shaping, complex logic gates, classifiers, oscillators, habituation, robust perfect adaptation, and noise reduction in stochastic settings. By turning specifications into families of circuit candidates, GenAI-Net provides a route to programmable biomolecular circuit design and accelerates translation from desired function to implementable mechanisms.

items.title: GENERATIVE AI ADOPTION BY SMES: DRIVERS, BARRIERS AND PERFORMANCE OUTCOMES IN NIGERIA
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is creating new opportunities for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to improve business processes, innovation, productivity, and competitiveness. However, the factors encouraging or limiting Generative AI adoption and its performance outcomes among SMEs in Nigeria remain underexplored. This study examines Generative AI adoption by SMEs in Nigeria, focusing on its drivers, barriers, and performance outcomes. A cross-sectional survey research design was employed, with data collected from 200 SME owners, managers, and employees using a structured questionnaire titled Generative AI Adoption and SME Performance Questionnaire (GAIA-SPQ), validated with a reliability coefficient of 0.86. Data were analyzed using correlation analysis at a 0.05 level of significance. Findings reveal that drivers of Generative AI significantly influence its adoption, while barriers also significantly affect adoption negatively. The study further finds that Generative AI use significantly affects SME performance, particularly in relation to productivity and innovation. The study concludes that Generative AI provides important opportunities for improving SME performance, although effective adoption requires favourable conditions and the reduction of implementation barriers. It is recommended that SMEs strengthen their technological capabilities, develop relevant digital skills, and adopt cost-effective Generative AI solutions to improve productivity, innovation, and competitiveness.

items.title: Generative AI in Islamic Education: A Maqāṣid-Based Framework for Curriculum, Assessment and Academic Integrity
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has entered Islamic schools, seminaries and universities faster than the institutions can govern it. Students use chatbots to explain verses, draft essays and prepare for examinations, while teachers lack shared rules on what is permitted, how to disclose it and how to assess learning fairly. This paper proposes a practical framework that grounds those decisions in the objectives of the Sharia (maqāṣid al-sharīʿa) rather than in generic ethics alone. Using an analytical synthesis of recent evidence on generative AI in education, research on assessment and academic integrity, international governance guidance, and the maqāṣid literature, the paper maps the five classical necessities (religion, life, intellect, lineage and property) onto the risks of AI-mediated learning and derives design principles for three layers: curriculum, assessment and academic integrity. The framework calls for AI literacy grounded in the ethic of verification, assessment built on authentic and oral demonstration of understanding instead of unreliable detection software, a three-tier policy on permitted use with disclosure, and governance that protects learner data and religious content. A phased implementation route and indicators are offered for institutions. The paper is conceptual and untested in practice; it closes with a research agenda for piloting the framework, comparing it across legal schools and measuring its effects on learning.

items.title: Generative AI-Assisted Competitive Microlearning Strategy: Development and Validation of the Plomp Model in Classroom Teacher Education in Finland
items.abstract: Background. The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education has created challenges in designing responsible and adaptive learning strategies. Meanwhile, competitive elements in gamified learning remain debated due to inconsistent effects on learner engagement. Purpose. This research aimed to develop and evaluate a generative AI-assisted competitive microlearning strategy for improving instructional media development skills among Finnish Luokanopettajakoulutus (Class Teacher Education) students. Novelty. This study introduces a novel instructional design that integrates generative AI, microlearning, and optional quality-based competition. Unlike conventional competitive gamification approaches, the proposed strategy recognizes learner differences by examining whether competition produces varied outcomes across learning groups Method. Using the Plomp development model, the study involved 79 undergraduate students from four parallel classes. Data from expert validation, practicality questionnaires, and product assessments were analyzed using Aiken’s V and descriptive statistics. Results. The strategy achieved high validity (Aiken’s V = 0.87) and strong practicality (83.1% student response; 85.9% lecturer response). Variation in competition participation (41–62%) indicated different effects among learner groups. Conclusion. The findings contribute an adaptive AI-assisted microlearning framework that balances innovation, learner diversity, and educational equity in teacher education.

items.title: Grand Theft Autocomplete: 'AI' enclosures and their threat to data sovereignty
items.abstract: The way we distribute research data and software today relies heavily on the open web: largely standardised formats, decentralised data hubs, public availability, affordable compute, free learning resources, and findability afforded by a few ad-supported web indexes. This openness, however, is increasingly under threat. The companies that currently attempt to monetise large language models also make it much harder to keep websites online and position their chat interfaces as intermediaries between knowledge and users. The ‘AI’-enclosed web empowers Big Tech to further interfere in learning, education, and research. This talk draws a parallel to the historical appropriation of common land in 18th- and 19th-century England. With this historical revolution of the rich against the poor to learn from, it outlines the specific dangers to the knowledge commons in the next few years. In conclusion, the talk attempts to identify what can be done to preserve and and empower individual, institutional, and transnational data sovereignty in the face of this not entirely new threat: critique the neoreactionary ideology behind the technology, empower ‘boring’ technology, identify affordable machine-learning tech, and embrace local and peer-to-peer computing.

items.title: Greco-Roman Wrestling and the Chronology of Physical Culture: Ethnocultural Traditions, Historical Continuity, and Pedagogical Perspectives
items.abstract: Physical culture, as a subcomponent of general culture, reflects the set of constructive manifestations of the human factor in the field of movement, integrating the progress of science, technology, art and medicine (Platonov, Vl., 2006). Within this theoretical framework, the present study aims to show the historical continuity and practical evolution of Greco-Roman wrestling as a specific expression of physical culture, analyzing the connections between socio-cultural development, advances in biomotor sciences and transformations of modern pedagogical paradigms. The paper offers an analytical approach that goes beyond general terminological observations, bringing the following contributions: 1) identifying the historical and socio-cultural stages that shaped the forms and functions of Greco-Roman wrestling; 2) integrating empirical evidence from biomotricity to explain the technical-tactical adaptations and physiological requirements of athletes; 3) formulating contemporary pedagogical directions for optimizing the technical-tactical and physical preparation process within combat training. Thus, the paper argues for the continuity of a specific sports tradition within the broader framework of physical culture and proposes practical and theoretical frameworks for integrating historical knowledge into the design of training and sports education programs.

items.title: GUIA uditor : Enabling Post-hoc Child Safety Forensics via Action-Guided GUI Provenance on Mobile Devices
items.abstract: The proliferation of smart devices exposes children to online risks like grooming and financial scams that are deeply embedded within legitimate applications. Current approaches rely on automated prevention and detection, a paradigm that is fundamentally limited by its inherent fallibility. Whether rule-based or AI-driven, they inevitably produce false positives and negatives, failing to provide reliable protection. In this paper, we argue for a complementary, human-in-the-loop, post-hoc forensic paradigm. We present GUIA uditor , the first system designed to realize this vision by creating GUI Provenance: a queryable, semantic record of a child's interaction sequence. To generate this, GUIA uditor leverages a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) to translate the temporal sequence of GUI events into a human-understandable narrative. To make this practical on mobile devices, a novel evidence distillation pipeline reduces the data requiring analysis by over 89.2% compared to periodic sampling approaches adopted by industry standards, with negligible impact on accuracy. On a new dataset of 295 interaction clips, GUIA uditor achieves a 95.23% Macro-F1 Score in logging significant events and, crucially, its two-stage forensic query engine successfully retrieves the correct evidence as the top result for over 90.20% of natural language questions. An end-to-end evaluation on three modern smartphones shows that the full pipeline, including on-device MLLM inference, adds 2.1W of power draw and 7.4s of per-event latency, with a peak memory footprint of ~3.1GB. These results show that post-hoc GUI forensics can run on modern mobile devices and provide useful context for guardian-led safety review.

items.title: Guiding Responsible AI Use in Scholarly Publishing and Communication: Introducing the L-O-C-A-D Checklist
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) become embedded in research and publishing workflows, the scholarly community faces growing pressure to ensure their responsible and transparent use. The L-O‑C‑A‑D (Limitations, Ownership, Confidentiality, Accuracy, and Disclosure) Checklist, developed at EDP Sciences, offers authors, reviewers, and editors a practical, evidence‑based framework to assess and document their use of AI tools throughout the research and publication process. The checklist builds on the conceptual model proposed by Dr. Zhou in his Scholarly Kitchen article on the risks, rewards, and responsibilities of AI in peer review, broadening it into an operational, user-friendly tool suitable for diverse research contexts. The L-O‑C‑A‑D Checklist integrates guidance from the European Data Protection Board (EDPB), the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE), the European Association of Science Editors (EASE), and the STM Integrity Hub to create a consolidated, practice‑oriented resource. The L-O‑C‑A‑D Checklist helps users identify and mitigate key risks associated with AI systems, including training‑data opacity, model drift, hallucinations, privacy vulnerabilities, copyright ambiguities, and accountability challenges. It prompts users to assess data quality, avoid sharing confidential or unpublished material, verifying model versions, and ensure meaningful mandatory human oversight. It provides structured guidance for transparent AI disclosure. By promoting transparency, reproducibility, and human accountability, the L‑O‑C‑A‑D Checklist supports the principles of Open Science and strengthens integrity within AI‑augmented scholarly communication. This poster introduces the checklist, its rationale, and its practical applications for responsible innovation across the research ecosystem. This checklist is intended as a practical resource for the scholarly community and to evolve through collaborative feedback. Comments and suggestions are welcome at selina.labarbera@edpsciences.org

items.title: Guiding Responsible AI Use in Scholarly Publishing and Communication: Introducing the L-O-C-A-D Checklist
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) become embedded in research and publishing workflows, the scholarly community faces growing pressure to ensure their responsible and transparent use. The L-O‑C‑A‑D (Limitations, Ownership, Confidentiality, Accuracy, and Disclosure) Checklist, developed at EDP Sciences, offers authors, reviewers, and editors a practical, evidence‑based framework to assess and document their use of AI tools throughout the research and publication process. The checklist builds on the conceptual model proposed by Dr. Zhou in his Scholarly Kitchen article on the risks, rewards, and responsibilities of AI in peer review, broadening it into an operational, user-friendly tool suitable for diverse research contexts. The L-O‑C‑A‑D Checklist integrates guidance from the European Data Protection Board (EDPB), the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE), the European Association of Science Editors (EASE), and the STM Integrity Hub to create a consolidated, practice‑oriented resource. The L-O‑C‑A‑D Checklist helps users identify and mitigate key risks associated with AI systems, including training‑data opacity, model drift, hallucinations, privacy vulnerabilities, copyright ambiguities, and accountability challenges. It prompts users to assess data quality, avoid sharing confidential or unpublished material, verifying model versions, and ensure meaningful mandatory human oversight. It provides structured guidance for transparent AI disclosure. By promoting transparency, reproducibility, and human accountability, the L‑O‑C‑A‑D Checklist supports the principles of Open Science and strengthens integrity within AI‑augmented scholarly communication. This poster introduces the checklist, its rationale, and its practical applications for responsible innovation across the research ecosystem. This checklist is intended as a practical resource for the scholarly community and to evolve through collaborative feedback. Comments and suggestions are welcome at selina.labarbera@edpsciences.org

items.title: Gunshots or Fireworks? Tracing the Spatial Diffusion of Digital Participatory Surveillance
items.abstract: The proliferation of consumer surveillance technologies and hyperlocal social media platforms reflects a broad sociotechnical shift in the ways ordinary citizens maintain community safety through their participatory surveillance. Recent qualitative research suggests that platform-based surveillance amplifies perceived neighborhood threat as residents adopt these tools to maintain urban order. How are these digital tools proliferating so rapidly despite historic declines in crime? To address this question, this article investigates the spatiotemporal diffusion of participatory surveillance across urban neighborhoods using dynamic spatial Durbin models with neighborhood and temporal fixed effects. The results show that participatory surveillance spreads through a self-reinforcing feedback loop in which surveillance activity clusters over time and propagates outward from early hotspots. These spatiotemporal patterns are consistent with a conceptual framework in which digital technologies localize a risk society by anchoring a diffuse sense of insecurity onto local spaces and legitimizing further informal social control. These findings have implications for understanding how surveillance technologies reshape perceptions of neighborhood disorder and reproduce urban inequality.

items.title: How do virtual exercise technology and social presence influence motivation to exercise?
items.abstract: Introduction Virtual technology offers a promising tool for encouraging engagement in exercise, as it can provide the user with enhanced visual stimuli and accessible metrics; however, the specific features within that technology that contribute to motivation and participation require further investigation. This study examined how different visual displays and the presence of a second rider influenced motivation to exercise using virtual technology. Methods Twenty-four young adults completed a 3-km cycling course on the same virtual track under three counterbalanced conditions including (a) a metrics-only ride, where a screen in front of the rider displayed only standard performance variables (e.g., power, cadence), (b) a solo-virtual ride, which was identical to the previous condition, but with the addition of the participant being depicted on the screen as an avatar amongst virtual scenery, and (c) a paired-virtual ride, that contained the same elements as the previous two conditions, but with the addition of a second rider represented on the screen as an avatar. Results The quantitative results, which included performance-related variables (cadence, power, speed, and heart rate), measures of intrinsic motivation, and ratings of perceived exertion, revealed significantly higher values for the paired-virtual condition compared to both the metrics-only and the solo-virtual conditions. Differences between the metrics-only and the solo-virtual conditions were isolated to interest-enjoyment and effort-importance. Brief interviews with participants indicated that the paired-virtual condition produced heightened levels of enjoyment and competitive drive which motivated participants to exert more effort. The solo-virtual condition was reported to be relaxing, but it was also reported as the least engaging. The metrics-only condition provoked negative emotions due to the absence of distractions and a heightened focus on internal cues. Discussion The results highlight the psychological mechanisms that influence motivation and engagement when using virtual exercise technology.

items.title: Human Factor Contributions to Accidents and Fatalities in U.S. Construction: A Comparative Analysis of Three Major Subsectors
items.abstract: Human factors remain a leading cause of occupational accidents and fatalities in the construction industry. Although human factors are a major contributor to construction accidents, their relative impact across different construction subsectors has not been fully quantified. This study presents a comparative analysis of accident and fatality data from the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) for three major construction subsectors, NAICS 236 (Construction of Buildings), 237 (Heavy and Civil Engineering Construction), and 238 (Specialty Trade Contractors) from January 2010 through June 2025. Seventy human-factor-related keywords were categorized into eight categories, and accident counts, fatality counts, and fatality rates, defined as the proportion of investigated cases that were fatal, were computed. Twenty-four high-frequency keywords (≥60 investigated accidents) were further analyzed across the three subsectors. Descriptive methods, including risk matrices, Pareto analysis, and category-level fatality rate comparisons, were applied to identify the factors contributing most to fatalities. Differences between subsectors were tested using permutation-based chi-square tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Results indicate substantial variation in both frequency and severity among keywords. At the category level, cognitive or perceptual errors, procedural violations and unsafe acts, and judgment and awareness failures in equipment use showed significantly higher fatality proportions in Heavy and Civil Engineering Construction than in the other two subsectors, whereas at the keyword level only lost balance and inattention differed significantly once the correction was applied. The findings provide a data-driven basis for prioritizing targeted safety interventions and tailoring human factor mitigation strategies to subsector-specific risks.

items.title: Human-Centered AI Education for Viksit Bharat @2047: Reimagining Teachers, Learners and Future-Ready Schools
items.abstract: Abstract: Artificial Intelligence is reshaping how societies function, communicate, learn and innovate, and India stands at a particularly consequential point in this shift. The arrival of generative AI, adaptive learning platforms and intelligent digital tools presents the country with both a rare opportunity and a demanding policy challenge on its path toward Viksit Bharat @2047. Education sits at the heart of this challenge, because the citizens, workers and innovators who will carry that vision forward are being shaped right now, inside today's classrooms. This conceptual paper asks how Artificial Intelligence can genuinely strengthen India's education system without eroding the human qualities that make learning meaningful: agency, creativity, ethics and social responsibility. Drawing on an integrative reading of policy documents and international literature - UNESCO's AI competency frameworks, OECD perspectives on AI literacy, India's National Education Policy 2020, the IndiaAI Mission, the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025, ILO research on generative AI and employment, and the author's own practitioner book AI and Us - the paper argues that the real question is not whether AI will replace teachers, but whether schools can build a working partnership between teachers, learners and AI. The paper introduces a Human-Centered AI Education Framework built around six interlocking dimensions: AI Literacy, AI-Augmented Pedagogy, Human Skills, Ethical and Responsible Use, Inclusive Digital Infrastructure, and Continuous Professional Learning. It also sketches a Teacher-AI-Student ecosystem in which AI takes on assistive and analytical work while teachers hold on to pedagogical, relational and ethical authority. Viksit Bharat @2047, the paper contends, does not just need citizens who are skilled at using AI - it needs citizens who are AI-literate, critical, creative, ethical and socially engaged. The paper closes with policy recommendations aimed at schools, teacher-education institutions, government bodies and educational technology developers.
